breakfast.name: Mofo Gasy (Malagasy Bread)
instructions: Mix batter, let rise 30 min
Pour into greased molds
Cook on flat griddle
Flip when golden
breakfast.description: Sweet rice flour griddle cakes — sold on every Madagascar street corner.

breakfast.name: Vary Amin'anana (Rice and Greens Soup)
instructions: Cook rice in extra water
Add greens, onion, ginger
Simmer until soupy porridge
breakfast.description: Rice soup with leafy greens — Malagasy everyday comfort.

breakfast.name: Mofo Akondro (Banana Fritters)
instructions: Mash ripe bananas into a paste
Mix with rice flour, coconut milk, sugar, cinnamon to form a thick batter
The riper the banana, the sweeter — no added sugar needed if using overripe
Fry spoonfuls in hot oil until golden
The outside should be crispy, the inside soft and banana-dense
Dust with cinnamon or powdered sugar if desired
Mofo akondro are Madagascar's breakfast banana fritters
Found at morning markets across the island
The rice flour (not wheat) gives a distinct texture — slightly grainy outside
Madagascar grows hundreds of banana varieties — the sweetness varies by region
breakfast.description: Madagascar's morning banana fritters — overripe bananas mashed into a rice flour batter and fried until crispy outside, soft and banana-intense inside. Rice flour instead of wheat flour gives a slightly grainy exterior that complements the dense banana center. Found at every morning market across the island.

breakfast.name: Vary Amin'anana (Rice with Greens)
ingredients: Mixed greens (cassava leaves, sweet potato leaves, or spinach)
Optional: dried shrimp or small fish for depth
instructions: Cook rice in a generous amount of water — Malagasy rice is cooked slightly wetter than East Asian rice
Wilt greens briefly in a pan with garlic and onion
Season simply: salt, pepper
In Madagascar, the dish is about the rice — the greens are the accompaniment, not the star
Optional: add dried shrimp or small fried fish for protein depth
The 'vary' (rice) is always the center of any Malagasy meal
Vary amin'anana means 'rice with greens' — the simplest version of the Malagasy meal
Eaten morning, noon, and night in rural Madagascar
The cassava leaves give an earthy, slight bitterness the spinach version lacks
Rice consumption in Madagascar is among the highest per capita in the world
breakfast.description: Madagascar's foundational rice-and-greens breakfast — rice cooked slightly wet alongside wilted cassava or sweet potato leaves with garlic. 'Vary' (rice) is the center of every Malagasy meal; the greens are the accompaniment. Eaten three times daily in rural areas. Madagascar has one of the world's highest per-capita rice consumption rates.

lunch.name: Romazava (Meat and Greens Stew)
instructions: Brown beef with onion and garlic
Add tomatoes and ginger
Add mixed greens
Simmer 30 min
Serve over rice
lunch.description: Madagascar's national dish — beef and mixed greens stew over rice.

lunch.name: Ravitoto (Cassava Leaf with Pork)
instructions: Pound and boil cassava leaves 30 min
Brown pork with garlic, ginger, onion
Combine with leaves and coconut milk
Simmer 20 min
Serve over rice
lunch.description: Pounded cassava leaves with pork in coconut milk.

lunch.name: Ravitoto sy Henakisoa (Cassava Leaves with Pork)
ingredients: Cassava leaves (pounded — this breaks the cell structure, releasing toxins safely)
instructions: CRITICAL: cassava leaves must be pounded and then cooked long to eliminate hydrogen cyanide
Pound leaves in a mortar — the pounding begins the cyanide breakdown
Cook pounded leaves in water for 30+ minutes — the long cooking eliminates toxins
Drain and rinse the cooked leaves
Fry pork with onion, garlic until cooked and slightly crispy at the edges
Add the cooked cassava leaves to the pork
Braise together 20-30 more minutes — the leaves absorb the pork fat
Season with salt and pepper
Optional: add coconut milk for richness
Ravitoto is Madagascar's beloved comfort dish — the leaves become dark green and silky
The pork fat absorbed into the cassava leaves is the flavor mechanism
lunch.description: Madagascar's comfort dish — pounded cassava leaves (the pounding is food-safety critical for cyanide breakdown) long-braised with pork belly until the leaves become dark, silky, and saturated with rendered pork fat. Ravitoto is Madagascar's most beloved dish: every region has it; every cook has their ratio. The dark green leaves and pork fat combination is the flavor of home.

lunch.name: Ro Mazava (Clear Vegetable Beef Broth)
ingredients: Water spinach or morning glory (or local greens)
instructions: Simmer beef bones and meat in water with garlic, onion, ginger — 30 minutes minimum
The broth should be clear and golden — not cloudy
Remove the meat, shred it back in
Add greens — water spinach, morning glory, or local Malagasy vegetables
Add tomatoes — they break down and add brightness
Season with salt — no soy or fish sauce — the flavor is pure and clean
Ro mazava (literally 'clear broth') is Madagascar's simple everyday soup
It is deliberately mild and clear — meant to be eaten with lots of rice
The rice goes in the bowl and the clear broth pours over
The clarity of the broth is the aesthetic ideal
lunch.description: Madagascar's clear everyday soup — bone-in beef simmered until the broth is golden and clear, with greens, tomato, and ginger. 'Ro mazava' translates to 'clear broth' — the clarity is intentional. Eaten poured over rice: the rice absorbs the mild, clean-tasting broth. Madagascar's deliberate restraint from heavy spicing makes the natural meat-vegetable flavor the focus.

dinner.name: Hen'omby sy Sakamalao (Beef with Ginger)
instructions: Brown beef
Add ginger, garlic, onion, tomatoes
Simmer 35 min
Serve over rice

dinner.name: Akoho sy Voanio (Chicken with Coconut)
instructions: Brown chicken
Add onion, garlic, ginger, tomatoes
Add coconut milk
Simmer 30 min
Serve over rice
dinner.description: Chicken simmered in coconut milk and ginger.

dinner.name: Henakisoa amin'ny Sakamalao (Pork with Ginger)
instructions: Pound ginger to release the oils — the intensity is important
Fry garlic in oil until fragrant
Add pork, stir-fry over high heat
Add pounded ginger — the fresh ginger fragrance fills the kitchen
Season with soy sauce — the Chinese influence on coastal Madagascar cuisine
The soy sauce and ginger combination reflects the Chinese trading community presence
Add spring onions at the end
The dish should have a fresh ginger bite — not a mild background note
Henakisoa amin'ny sakamalao is weeknight pork — quick, fragrant, satisfying
Served always with vary (rice) — the pork is the flavoring, rice is the meal
dinner.description: Madagascar's ginger pork — thin pork pieces stir-fried with pounded fresh ginger and soy sauce. The soy sauce reflects Chinese trading community influence on Madagascar's coastal cuisine (Chinese traders arrived in the 18th century). The fresh ginger is not a background note — it's the dish's identity, fragrant and sharp.

dinner.name: Akoho sy Voanio (Chicken in Coconut Milk)
ingredients: Coconut milk (fresh — Madagascar's coconut is excellent)
instructions: Marinate chicken briefly in garlic, turmeric, salt
Fry chicken in oil until the skin is golden
Add coconut milk — it should almost submerge the chicken
Add onion, optional lemongrass or lime leaf
Braise on medium heat 30-35 minutes — the coconut milk reduces slightly
The sauce should coat the chicken without being thick curry
Season with salt, optional chili
The coconut milk from Madagascar's east coast coconuts is rich and naturally sweet
Akoho sy voanio is coastal Madagascar's chicken dish
The simplicity — coconut milk, chicken, garlic, turmeric — lets the coconut quality show
The east coast of Madagascar has extensive coconut groves along the ocean
dinner.description: Madagascar's coconut chicken — chicken braised gently in coconut milk with turmeric and garlic. Madagascar's east coast coconuts are notably rich and sweet; the simplicity of this dish lets their quality show. No heavy spicing — the coconut is the sauce, not a background ingredient. Coastal Madagascar's definitive chicken preparation.

snacks.name: Sambos (Samosas)
ingredients: Filling: ground beef, onion, ginger, garlic
instructions: Make dough, cut strips
Fill with spiced beef
Fold triangles, seal
Fry until golden

snacks.name: Koba (Peanut-Banana Rice Cake)
instructions: Toast rice flour lightly in a dry pan
Mix toasted rice flour with mashed banana, ground peanuts, palm sugar
The mixture should be a thick, sticky dough
Lay banana leaves flat — soften them briefly over flame to make them pliable
Place portions of dough on the banana leaf
Wrap tightly — the banana leaf is the cooking vessel
Steam the wrapped koba for 45-60 minutes
The koba firms up inside the leaf — it's dense and chewy
Cool before unwrapping — the banana leaf imparts a subtle vegetal fragrance
Koba is sold by street vendors — triangular or cylindrical banana leaf packets
The peanut-banana combination is Madagascar's sweetness signature
snacks.description: Madagascar's peanut-banana rice cake — glutinous rice flour mixed with mashed banana, ground peanuts, and palm sugar, wrapped in banana leaves and steamed. The banana leaf imparts a subtle vegetal fragrance. Dense, chewy, and sweet: koba is Madagascar's most iconic street snack, sold in neat banana leaf packets by vendors across the island.

snacks.name: Mofo Gasy Frit (Fried Rice Cakes)
instructions: Same batter as mofo gasy (see breakfast) — but fried rather than griddle-cooked
The frying gives a different texture: crispy outside, airy inside
The yeast creates bubbles in the batter as it fries
They puff slightly in the oil
Drain on paper — serve immediately while crispy
The fried version is the snack form; the griddle version is breakfast
Mofo gasy frit vendors often set up near schools and markets
The coconut-rice smell of frying mofo is Madagascar's most recognizable street food fragrance
The same batter transforms dramatically between the griddle and the fryer
snacks.description: Madagascar's fried rice cake — the same rice flour-coconut milk-yeast batter as mofo gasy, but deep-fried instead of griddle-cooked. The frying creates a crispy exterior and puffed interior entirely different from the griddle version. The same batter, two different textures. Found near schools and markets as an afternoon snack.

snacks.name: Fried Cassava (Manioc Frit)
instructions: Peel cassava carefully — the outer skin contains cyanide compounds
Cube or slice into thick pieces
Boil first until just barely cooked through — 10 minutes
Drain and dry completely — the drying is essential for crispy frying
Fry in hot oil until golden and crispy on the outside
The inside should be floury and soft
Season with salt immediately from the oil
Cassava is Madagascar's backup staple when rice is scarce
The crispy fried cassava is a common roadside snack
The texture is between potato and yuca (same plant, different names)
Cassava frit is also a side dish alongside fish or chicken
snacks.description: Madagascar's roadside cassava snack — parboiled cassava cubes fried until crispy outside and floury-soft inside. Cassava is Madagascar's insurance crop: when rice (the primary staple) is scarce or expensive, cassava feeds the island. Fried cassava is the immediate, accessible snack version, sold from roadside stalls.

snacks.name: Sakamalao Candy (Crystallized Ginger)
instructions: Slice young ginger thinly or into small pieces
Boil in sugar syrup until the ginger becomes translucent
Remove from syrup, roll in dry sugar
Allow to dry and crystallize — the sugar coating hardens
The ginger heat is somewhat mellowed by the sugar but still present
Madagascar grows significant amounts of ginger — it's an export crop
Crystallized ginger is a traditional Malagasy sweet and digestive aid
Children eat it as candy; adults take it as a remedy for stomach upset
The sweet-hot combination is addictive — the lingering ginger warmth after the sugar
snacks.description: Madagascar's crystallized ginger sweet — sliced young ginger cooked in sugar syrup, rolled in dry sugar, and dried into candy. Madagascar is a significant ginger producer; the candy version is both a traditional sweet and a folk remedy for nausea. The sweet exterior and lingering ginger heat is the combination that makes it compelling as both candy and cure.

desserts.name: Godro-Godro (Coconut Flan)
instructions: Mix rice flour with coconut milk, sugar, vanilla, eggs
Pour into mold
Steam or bake 30 min
Serve at room temperature

desserts.name: Bonbon Coco (Coconut Candy)
instructions: Combine grated coconut, sugar, small amount of water in a pan
Cook over medium heat, stirring constantly
As water evaporates, the mixture becomes thick and sticky
Continue cooking until it masses together and pulls from the sides of the pan
Shape quickly while hot — roll into balls or press into shapes
They cool and firm into a sweet, coconut-dense candy
Bonbon coco is Madagascar's most beloved sweet — homemade and sold by vendors
Often made in colored varieties — the food coloring distinguishes flavors (pink=rose, green=pandan)
The grated coconut holds its texture even when candied
Sold in small bags or individual pieces wrapped in paper
desserts.description: Madagascar's coconut candy — freshly grated coconut cooked with sugar until the mixture masses together, shaped into balls or pieces while hot. The grated coconut texture survives the candy-making process: each piece is dense with actual coconut strands. Made in colors (pink, green) that signal flavor additions. Madagascar's most ubiquitous sweet.

desserts.name: Vary Amin'ny Ronono (Sweet Rice Pudding)
ingredients: Vanilla bean (Madagascar vanilla — among the world's best)
instructions: Cook rice in coconut milk — the coconut milk replaces water
As it cooks, the rice absorbs the coconut richness
Add sugar, scraped vanilla bean — Madagascar vanilla is complex and deeply fragrant
The vanilla fragrance intensifies as the rice cooks
Stir frequently as it thickens — like risotto
Optional: finish with cinnamon
Serve warm or cold — both are correct
Madagascar produces 80%+ of the world's vanilla — the vanilla in this rice pudding is one of the finest available anywhere
The irony: vanilla-rich Madagascar uses vanilla primarily in local sweet rice pudding and exported globally
The coconut-vanilla-rice combination is Madagascar's quintessential dessert
desserts.description: Madagascar's vanilla rice pudding — rice cooked in coconut milk with sugar and Madagascar vanilla bean. Madagascar produces over 80% of the world's vanilla supply, making this the home of the finest vanilla rice pudding on earth. The fragrant, deep vanilla paired with rich coconut milk and tender rice is Madagascar's definitive sweet.

drinks.name: Ranonapango (Burned Rice Water)
instructions: Add water to the burned rice crust in the pot
Boil 5 min
Strain and serve
drinks.description: Tea made from the burned rice crust — uniquely Malagasy.

drinks.name: Toaka Gasy (Rice Rum)
instructions: Cook rice, mix with sugarcane
Ferment 5-7 days
Distill

drinks.name: Ranon'ampango (Rice Water Tea)
ingredients: Rice (the scorched rice left in the pot after cooking — called 'ampango')
instructions: After rice is cooked, a thin layer is often scorched to the bottom of the pot in Madagascar — this is intentional
Pour boiling water over the scorched rice in the pot
Let steep 5-10 minutes
Pour off the liquid — it's lightly golden and slightly smoky from the scorched rice
This is ranon'ampango — the Malagasy rice water tea
It's not wasted — it's the drink that accompanies the meal
Mild, slightly sweet from the starches, with a toasty note from the caramelized rice
Ranon'ampango is consumed by most Malagasy households daily
It's both a drink and a pot-cleaning technique
Zero waste: the pot's residue becomes the family beverage
drinks.description: Madagascar's daily rice tea — boiling water poured over intentionally scorched rice left in the cooking pot, steeped until the water turns golden and faintly smoky. Zero waste: the pot cleans itself, and the family gets a mild, slightly sweet, toasty drink. Most Malagasy households drink ranon'ampango at every meal. A deliberate scorching technique, not an accident.
